fields.meta_description: Build a mystery reader sign up sheet that books one reader per Friday and hides the name from other families, with clues sent to the teacher.
fields.h1: Build a Mystery Reader Sign-Up Sheet That Keeps the Secret
fields.hero_description: Build a mystery reader sign up sheet that gives each reader one Friday and keeps the name hidden from other families.
fields.features_heading: What the Sheet Handles Before Story Time
fields.features_subheading: A printed grid holds a date and a name. Build the sheet with Emergent, and the app also keeps the secret and sends the clues.
fields.feature_1:
One reader for each Friday

List the term's Fridays, each at 2:30 PM, and let a family book one. A booked Friday closes to everyone else, and no two grandparents turn up at the door for one slot.
fields.feature_2:
Taken dates without names

Families see a booked Friday as taken and nothing more. The reader's name stays on the teacher's dashboard, out of sight of a child who might spot it on a parent's phone.
fields.feature_3:
Three clue boxes on every sign-up

Ask each reader for three clues about themselves, such as a job or the town they grew up in. The app emails them to the teacher on Thursday morning, a day before the visit.
fields.feature_4:
A check against books already read

Ask for the title the reader plans to bring. If the class heard it earlier in the term, the form shows the date it was read, and the reader can choose a different book.
fields.feature_5:
Reminders two days ahead

Each reader gets an email on Wednesday, two days before the visit, with the arrival time and the teacher's check-in note. Canceling takes one link and frees the Friday.
fields.feature_6:
A record of who has had a turn

See each child next to their reader's date, with children still waiting at the top. Sign-ups sit in a database you own, and paid plans export the full code to GitHub.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Classrooms Book Their Readers
fields.tab_content_1:
No family sees who took November 6

Fridays at Oakbrindle Elementary's kindergarten end with a mystery reader at 2:30 PM, one per week. Gaspard Rauschen books November 6 to read to his daughter's class. When other parents open the sheet, November 6 shows as taken with no name beside it. His daughter scrolls her mom's phone and learns nothing.
fields.tab_content_2:
Clues from every reader reach Ms. Kestermann a day early

Thursday morning, Ms. Kestermann at Corvally Elementary opens an email with three clues about Friday's first grade reader. The reader typed them at sign-up, starting with I fly planes for a living. The class hears one clue at a time on Friday and guesses before the door opens.
fields.tab_content_3:
Each title read this term shows its date

Grandma Leopoldine Gwillim books November 13 with her grandson's second grade class at Fenwyck Elementary and types Where the Wild Things Are. The form tells her the class heard it on October 2. She switches to The Day the Crayons Quit, a title no reader has brought this term.
fields.tab_content_4:
Four families still waiting hear of every reopened Friday

By November, 18 of the 22 children in Pemberwick Elementary's third grade have had a mystery reader. Then the reader booked for November 20 cancels with the link in her reminder. The Friday reopens, and the app emails the families of the 4 children still waiting. The Sallowby family books it within the hour.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Mystery Reader Sign-Up Sheet
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up a mystery reader sign up sheet that fills every Friday and keeps each reader a surprise, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick one weekday and a time near the end of a lesson, such as Fridays at 2:30 PM. Give each visit about 20 minutes, enough for one picture book and the guessing. List every Friday of the term before you share the sheet.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Let parents, grandparents, and older siblings sign up, and ask how each reader is related to the child. Call the front office before you open the sheet and ask what a visitor needs to bring to check in.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write three clue prompts that hint without naming, such as the town a reader grew up in or the work they do. Add a note asking readers to leave their name and their child's name out of every clue.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Add a field for the title, with a box to tick when a reader wants the teacher to choose one from the class shelf. Keep the term's titles in one list. A book the class already heard then gets flagged at sign-up.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write one prompt with the Fridays, the clue boxes, the book field, and who may see the reader's name. Emergent builds the sheet and its database. To change it mid-term, describe the change in another prompt.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Set reminders and the cancel rule
fields.howto_step_6_des: Put a cancel link in every reminder, so a reader who falls ill can free the date in one tap. Decide who hears about a canceled Friday: the families of children still waiting, or the whole class list.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Book two Fridays from two browsers, one as yourself and one as a test grandparent who types a title from the read list. Check that each view shows the other date as taken with no name. Then delete both test rows.

faq_plan.q: What is a mystery reader sign up sheet?
faq_plan.a: A mystery reader sign up sheet is a schedule where family members book a date to read a book to a child's class without the children knowing who is coming. Before the visit, the teacher reads the class clues about the reader, and the children guess whose parent or grandparent it is.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a mystery reader sign up sheet?
faq_plan.a: Write a prompt that lists the term's Fridays and the clue boxes, and say who may see each reader's name. Emergent's AI form builder turns that prompt into the sheet, with a database behind it. Book a test Friday yourself, then send the link to families.

faq_plan.q: Which questions belong on a mystery reader sign up sheet?
faq_plan.a: Ask for the reader's name, phone number, email, and relationship to the child, plus the Friday they want. Add three clue boxes and a book title field, with an option for the teacher to supply the book. In the app Emergent builds, every answer lands in a database you own, not on a sheet taped to the classroom door.

faq_plan.q: How does a mystery reader sign up sheet keep the reader a secret?
faq_plan.a: It shows booked dates as taken without a name and sends the clues to the teacher alone. Ask readers to keep the visit quiet at home and to come to the front office, not the classroom door. In the app Emergent builds, the reader's name sits on the teacher's dashboard and nowhere else.

faq_plan.q: How many clues should a mystery reader sign up sheet ask for?
faq_plan.a: Ask for three, ordered from hardest to easiest. Read them one at a time and let the class guess after each. Save the easiest clue, such as I drive a red pickup truck, for last, after the children have had two tries.

faq_plan.q: Should a mystery reader sign up sheet say how long each visit lasts?
faq_plan.a: Yes: say about 20 minutes in all. Ask readers to pick a book that reads aloud in under 10 minutes, which leaves time for the reveal and a few questions from the class. Repeat the length in the confirmation email to keep chapter books at home.

faq_plan.q: How many dates should a mystery reader sign up sheet offer?
faq_plan.a: Offer at least as many dates as there are children in the class. Count the children and the Fridays left: a class of 22 with one reader a week needs 22 Fridays. If fewer Fridays remain than children, add a second slot on some Fridays.

faq_plan.q: Can a mystery reader sign up sheet include video visits?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if the teacher can put a video call on the classroom screen. Add a choice on the sheet for in person or by video, and ask Emergent to put the call link in the reminder email. A grandparent three states away still gets a Friday.

faq_plan.q: How do I make sure every child gets a turn on the mystery reader sign up sheet?
faq_plan.a: Check who is still waiting a month before the term ends, and contact those families directly. For a child whose family cannot come, offer a stand-in, such as the principal or the school librarian. Keep the stand-in's visit a surprise too, with clues like any other reader's.

faq_plan.q: What happens when someone cancels on a mystery reader sign up sheet?
faq_plan.a: Offer the reader a later Friday first, then open their date to the families still waiting. Keep a short picture book in the classroom and a stand-in you can call the same morning, in case a reader cancels on the day.

plan.angle: The top 10 for mystery reader sign up sheet is printables from Teachers Pay Teachers, Etsy, Scribd and Pinterest plus one generic online sign-up tool: a grid of dates and a line for a name. This page shows the sheet as the app that runs a term of readers: one reader per Friday with taken dates hidden from other families, three clues that reach the teacher the morning before, a book field that flags titles the class already heard, and a cancellation that reopens the date for children still waiting. The how-to and FAQ add what printables skip: who may sign up, how long a visit runs, and how to give every child a turn.
